keyPoints: Two failure modes with one root cause (uncurated context): bloat (raw tool dumps, stale results, long histories) and drift (the model loses its grip on the original task).
Prune tool output at the tool boundary — if the agent needs three fields from a 5,000-token payload, three fields is what enters context.
Compaction condenses older history into a running summary preserving decisions, key facts, and open questions.
Isolate context-hungry subtasks in subagents that return only distilled results; chain workflow steps with fresh contexts and distilled artifacts.
Track context size per turn and compact on a threshold, not on visible symptoms.
objectives.watchFor: A bigger context window only fits more noise — attention dilution is cured by curation. Compacting too aggressively trades bloat for amnesia, so summaries must keep load-bearing state.

question.stem: A long-running research agent slows down, repeats work, and starts ignoring its original instructions after many tool calls that each returned full API payloads. What is the right fix?
options: Move to a model with a larger context window
Prune tool results to task-relevant fields at the tool boundary and compact older history into a summary that preserves decisions and open questions
Reset the session whenever quality visibly degrades
Repeat the original instructions in every turn so they stay salient
question.answerWhy: These are bloat-and-drift symptoms from uncurated context, so the fix works at the source: trim payloads before they enter context and compact history while retaining load-bearing state. A larger window fits more noise without restoring attention, a hard reset discards the decisions the session established, and re-injecting instructions adds to the volume that caused the dilution.

keyPoints: Durable behavior (role, tone, policy, scope) belongs in the system prompt; variable per-request content belongs in user turns — this also keeps the prefix cacheable.
Delimit multi-part prompts with XML-style tags and reference those tags in the instructions so every span has an explicit role.
Structured reliability comes from explicit output constraints (schemas, closed enums, null-for-missing conventions) plus few-shot examples — not exhortation.
Sanitize untrusted input: delimit it, declare it data-only, and screen for boundary-breaking patterns.
Iterate systematically — representative test set, one change at a time, version every revision.
objectives.watchFor: "Double-check your work" and "be careful" are pleading, not specification; and tool-selection guidance belongs in tool names and descriptions, which is what the model actually reads when choosing.

question.stem: An extraction prompt sometimes omits required fields and sometimes invents values for absent ones. Which change is most likely to fix it?
options: Specify an explicit schema with required fields and a null-for-missing rule, and add few-shot examples including a case with an absent field
Add an instruction to be thorough and never guess
Move the input document into the system prompt so it carries more authority
Raise the temperature so the model explores more complete answers
question.answerWhy: Explicit output constraints plus a demonstration of the missing-field case give the model an unambiguous contract for both structure and edge behavior. Exhortation does not close a specification gap, moving the document into the system prompt erases the trusted/untrusted boundary and breaks caching, and a higher temperature increases variance rather than completeness.

keyPoints: Treat model output as untrusted input: parse defensively (responses may arrive wrapped in fences or prose), then validate.
Syntax is not safety — a response can parse cleanly while carrying a bad enum, an impossible quantity, or a hallucinated identifier.
Validate structure (required fields, types) and values (ranges, closed lists, referential existence) before anything downstream consumes it.
Every validation needs a defined failure path: corrective reprompt with the error, fallback, or human review — never silent pass-through.
Constrain structure at generation time with a schema or prefill so output is machine-consumable by construction.
objectives.watchFor: Confident tone carries no evidentiary weight, and using a second model call to check syntax a deterministic validator handles perfectly wastes money — save model review for judgments code cannot make.

question.stem: An order service parses Claude's JSON successfully but occasionally writes a shipment ID that does not exist in the database. What is missing?
options: A retry loop that regenerates the response until parsing succeeds
Value-level validation — closed lists, ranges, and referential checks such as confirming the shipment ID exists — with a defined failure path
A more capable model tier to reduce hallucinated identifiers
A second Claude call to review the JSON for correctness before writing
question.answerWhy: The payload is syntactically valid but semantically wrong, which is exactly the gap value-level validation closes — including a referential check against the system of record before any write. Retrying on parse success never triggers, a stronger model reduces but does not eliminate fabricated IDs, and a model-based reviewer is a probabilistic substitute for a lookup code can perform exactly.
